title: Multivariate quantum signal processing with optimal query complexity
authors: Mingrui Jing, Xin Wang, Zhan Yu, Lei Zhang
abstract: Polynomial transformations of data encoded in quantum operations are a building block of quantum algorithms, and their query complexity measures how often those operations are used. For multiple variables, existing methods either realize restricted polynomial families or implement monomials separately at a query cost exponential in the number of variables. We present a quantum circuit that implements every multivariate trigonometric polynomial up to an explicit normalization. The circuit processes one variable coherently over the frequency components of the remaining variables, allowing all components to share the same signal queries. Each variable is queried exactly as many times as its degree in the polynomial, and we prove that this query complexity is optimal. We further extend the construction to commuting unitaries. The resulting circuit applies the multivariate polynomial simultaneously across their shared eigenbasis, using the minimum numbers of forward and inverse queries to each unitary. We also study trainable rotations with fixed preparation and a local readout of the last input. At query depth at least two, independent uniform initialization gives every active readout gradient a variance lower bound set by its squared branch weight and the inverse square root of the depth, uniformly over data states and dimensions. For supervised squared loss, retaining sample correlations gives an initialization gradient-variance bound in terms of targets and input spectra. This also bounds the expected loss decrease after the first exact gradient step with a specified step size. These results provide a scalable and practical solution for developing multivariate quantum algorithms and quantum learning models.
summary: This paper develops advanced techniques for simulating multivariate polynomial transformations in quantum circuits, achieving optimal query complexity for both continuous variables and discrete unitaries. It also provides a deep theoretical framework using SDP duality to precisely quantify the minimum resources needed to realize such operations within a fixed quantum hardware workspace.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently implementing general multivariate polynomial transformations of quantum signals or unitaries while minimizing the required number of quantum queries.
main_result: It presents quantum circuits that achieve optimal query complexity for realizing multivariate trigonometric polynomials and extends this to commuting unitaries. Furthermore, it establishes rigorous mathematical criteria (via SDP duality) for determining the minimum required normalization for such operations in fixed-workspace quantum signal processing.
method: The methods involve constructing specialized quantum circuits using frequency component sharing for polynomial simulation, and employing Semidefinite Programming (SDP) duality theory to characterize the achievable quantum signal processing norm.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum signals defined by multivariate trigonometric polynomials $P(\mathbf{x})$ or transformations of commuting unitaries $P(\mathbf{U})$. The analysis is framed within quantum circuit complexity and quantum learning models.
key_observables: Query complexity (minimum number of times each input operation is used), gradient variance, and the quantum signal processing measure $\Gamma_\chi(P)$.
important_parameters: The degree of the polynomial, the number of variables ($N$), the depth of the circuit, and the fixed workspace dimension ($D$).
main_assumptions: For learning analysis, independent uniform initialization is assumed for gradient variance bounds. For signal processing, the analysis relies on strong duality theorems for SDPs and the existence of specific rank constraints for exact realization.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from constructing circuits for polynomial simulation with optimal query complexity to analyzing gradient variance in quantum learning. It then delves into the rigorous mathematical characterization of quantum signal processing capability using SDP duality and deriving exact, non-convex feasibility criteria for fixed-workspace realization.
why_interesting: The work provides fundamental tools for designing efficient quantum algorithms by providing tight bounds on resource costs (queries) and characterizing the limits of quantum computation in constrained physical settings.
